'''''Felicia amelloides''''', the '''blue daisy bush''', '''blue felicia''' or '''kingfisher daisy''', is a hairy, soft, usually [[Perennial plant|perennial]], [[evergreen]] plant, in the family [[Asteraceae]]. It can be found along the southern coast of [[South Africa]]. It grows as [[groundcover]], and is cultivated as an ornamental, where it was introduced in Europe in the middle of the 18th century.<ref name=Grau73>{{cite journal|first= J.|last= Grau|year= 1973|title= Revision der Gattung Felicia (Asteraceae)|journal= Mitteilungen der Botanischer Staatssammlung München|volume= IX|pages= 492–496|url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/15019162#page/508/mode/1up|access-date= 2017-11-12}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= Operation Wildflower|title= Felicia amelloides|author= Ivan Latti|url= https://www.operationwildflower.org.za/index.php/albums/genera-a-f/felicia/felicia-amelloides-907}}</ref>

[[Image:The Botanical Magazine, Plate 249 (Volume 7, 1794).png|thumb|right|Etching from The Botanical Magazine, published in 1794]]
[[Image:Botanischer Garten Funchal - Felicia amelloides IMG 1767.JPG|thumb|Variegated cultivar]]
== Description ==
''Felicia amelloides'' is an evergreen, rich and regularly branched, upright [[Perennial plant|perennial]], sometimes [[biennial plant|biennial]], [[herbaceous plant]] with a woody base, of about {{cvt|50|cm|ft}}, sometimes up to 1 m high plant. All of its leaves are [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|oppositely arranged]] along the stem, are usually relatively large, 2–5{{frac|1|2}} cm ({{frac|3|4}}–2 in) long and 1–2{{frac|1|2}} cm (0.4–1.0 in) wide, but strongly varying in size. They are elliptic to [[Glossary of botanical terms#obovate|inverted egg-shaped]], with a blunt or indistinctly pointy tip, an entire margin, and the leaves near the ground may have a short [[Peduncle (botany)|stalk]]. The leaves are stiff and leathery and feel sandpapery, due to a covering of short bristle-like hairs. Each leaf has one to three conspicuous veins, its margins are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#revolute|curled downwards]]. The upper surface is dark green, but the underside is lighter.<ref name=Grau73 />

===Inflorescences===
The [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|flower heads]] are about {{cvt|3|cm|frac=5}} across and sit individually on top of green to dark reddish, about {{cvt|18|cm|frac=2}} long, densely hairy [[Peduncle (botany)|stalks]]. The [[Bract#Involucral bracts|involucre]] is {{cvt|5–7|mm}} in diameter, and consist of two strict rows of bracts of {{cvt|8–11|mm}} long. The outer bracts are {{cvt|1–2|mm}} wide, narrowly [[Glossary of leaf morphology#oblanceolate|inverted lance-shaped]] with rough and sometimes also glandular hairs. The inner bracts are {{cvt|2–3|mm}} wide, inverted lance-shaped, with dry papery edges. The approximately twelve, bright blue, female [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|ray florets]] have a strap of about {{cvt|17|mm}} long and {{cvt|4|mm}} wide. These surround many [[Plant reproductive morphology#Terminology|bisexual]], disc florets with a yellow [[Petal#Corolla)|corolla]] of about {{cvt|4|mm}} long. 

In the center of each corolla are five [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] merged into a tube, through which the [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] grows when the floret opens, hoovering up the [[pollen]] on its shaft. At the tip of both style branches is a triangular appendage. Around the base of the corolla are many white, toothed, persistent [[Pappus (botany)|pappus bristles]] of about {{cvt|4|mm}} long, which become slightly wider towards the top. The eventually dark brown, dry, one-seeded, [[Dehiscence (botany)|indehiscent]] fruits called [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|cypselae]] are inverted egg-shaped, about {{cvt|4|mm}} long and {{cvt|2|mm}} wide, the surface slightly scaly, and covered with short hairs.<ref name=Grau73 /><ref name=PZA>{{cite web|website= SANBI PlantZAfrica|author= S.J. Smithies|title= Felicia amelloides|url= http://pza.sanbi.org/felicia-amelloides}}</ref>

''Felicia amelloides'' is a [[Ploidy#Diploid|diploid]] having nine sets of homologue chromosomes (2n=18).<ref name=Grau73 />

=== Differences with related species ===
The blue daisy can be distinguished from other Felicia species by the fact that all its leaves are opposite, with an entire margin, the plants have a very regular branching, and the involucral bracts are very long. Other Felicia species with only opposite leaves are ''[[Felicia denticulata|F. denticulata]]'', ''[[Felicia cymbalariae|F. cymbalariae]]'' (toothed leaves), ''[[Felicia joubertinae|F. joubertinae]]'' (small and narrow leaves) and ''[[Felicia flaneganii|F. flaneganii]]'' (small, obovate, petioled leaves).<ref name=Grau73 />

== Taxonomy and naming ==
The blue daisy was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in the second edition of his [[Species Plantarum]], published in 1763, and he named it ''Cineraria amelloides''. [[Conrad Moench]] gave it the name ''Cineraria oppositifolia'' in 1794, [[Henri Cassini]] called it ''Agathaea coelestris'' in 1815, while [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] reassigned Linnaeus’ name, creating ''Agathaea amelloides'' in 1836. Finally, Linnaeus’ specimen was moved by [[Andreas Voss (botanist)|Andreas Voss]], who so created ''Felicia amelloides'', the currently recognised name. Meanwhile, [[Carl Thunberg]] had [[Plant collecting|collected]] another specimen which he named ''Aster rotundifolius'' in 1800. In 1833 [[Christian Gottfried Daniel Nees von Esenbeck|Nees van Esenbeck]] reassigned Thunberg's plant and created ''Agathaea capensis''. [[William Henry Harvey]] ''Aster capensis'' [[variety (botany)|var.]] ''rotundifolius'' in 1865. In his 1973 ''[[Taxonomy (biology)#Monograph and taxonomic revision|Revision]] of the genus Felicia (Asteraceae)'', [[Jürke Grau]] regarded all of these name [[Synonymy (taxonomy)|synonymous]]. The species is the [[Type species]] of the [[Section (botany)|section]] [[Felicia (plant)#Neodetris|Neodetris]].<ref name=Grau73 />

''Aster capensis'' is a synonym for ''Felicia aethiopica'', not of ''F. amelloides''.<ref name=Grau73 />

The species [[epithet]] ''amelloides'' means "like ''[[Amellus]]''", which is a similar genus that also occurs in South Africa. ''Felicia amelloides'' has several common names including '''blue felicia''', '''bush felicia''', '''blue felicia bush''', '''blue daisy bush''', '''shrubby felicia''', '''Paris daisy''', and '''blue marguerite''' in English and '''''bloumagriet''''' or '''''blou-astertjie''''' in [[Afrikaans]]. The use of these names is not necessarily restricted to ''F. amelloides'' though.<ref name=PZA />

== Distribution, habitat and ecology ==
The blue daisy can be found in a strip along the south coast of the [[Western Cape]] and [[Eastern Cape]] provinces of South Africa, from [[De Hoop Nature Reserve]] in the west to the [[Kei Mouth|mouth of the Kei River]] in the east. It extends furthest inland in the Eastern Cape at the Vanstadensberg near [[Port Elizabeth]], the [[Groot Winterhoek|Groot Winterhoek Mountains]] near [[Uitenhage]], and the [[Ecca Pass]], on the road between [[Grahamstown]] and [[Fort Beaufort]]. The species is particularly common between [[Humansdorp]] and [[Port Alfred]]. The species does not occur on the Cape Peninsula, where it has been confused with ''[[Felicia aethiopica]]'', with similar flower heads but alternately set leaves above the base.

The blue daisy is most common on old stabilizing sand dunes, or where shelter is provided, but also occurs on sandy flats, gravelly slopes, stony hillsides, rock slabs and [[Table Mountain Sandstone]] outcrops, at {{cvt|0–1000|m|ft}} altitude.<ref name=PZA />

== Conservation ==
The continued survival of ''Felicia amelloides'' is considered to be of [[Least-concern species|least concern]] because its population is stable.<ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia amelloides|url= http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-5}}</ref>

== Use ==
''Felicia amelloides'' is used as an ornamental, both in South Africa and elsewhere. It was introduced to Europe during the eighteenth century and was one of the earliest species in [[horticulture]]. It survives some frost provided the soil is well draining, but dislikes moist heat. In hot climates, flowering ceases during summer. In colder climates, it is often treated as an annual, is sheltered in greenhouses or grown as a house plant.<ref name=PZA /><ref name=sav>{{cite web|website=SA-Venues|title= Felicia amelloides|url= https://www.sa-venues.com/plant-life/felicia-amelloides.php}}</ref>
